category.name: Git
category.description: Staging and commits, branches and merging, remotes, history rewriting and recovery, workflows and Git internals.

questions.text: The central server hosting your team's repository goes offline for a day. What can you still do in your full local clone?
options: Browse the whole history and make new commits, then push them later
View only the latest snapshot, because older history is fetched on demand
Make new commits, but git log shows only commits created since the outage
Read files only, because commits must be registered with the server first
questions.explanation: Git is distributed: a full clone holds every commit locally, so history browsing and committing work offline. Only operations that talk to the remote, such as fetch and push, need the server.

questions.text:
You run the commands below. Which content of notes.txt ends up in the new commit?

echo "draft 1" > notes.txt
git add notes.txt
echo "draft 2" > notes.txt
git commit -m "Add notes"
options: draft 2, because git commit reads files from the working tree
draft 1, because git commit records what is in the index
Nothing, because the file changed after it was staged
Both versions, stored as two separate commits
questions.explanation: A commit is built from the index. The second edit exists only in the working tree, so after the commit git status --short still shows M notes.txt.

questions.text: What does a Git commit object actually point to?
options: A diff of the lines that changed since its parent commit
A copy of the whole working directory, including untracked files
A tree holding a full snapshot of the tracked files, plus parents and metadata
Only the files that were staged for that particular commit
questions.explanation: git cat-file -p HEAD shows a tree line (the complete snapshot), parent lines, author, committer and message. Diffs are computed on the fly when you compare two snapshots.

questions.text: report.txt has a change that is staged and a different change that is not. You run git restore --staged report.txt. What happens?
options: Both changes are discarded and the file matches the last commit
The unstaged change is discarded and the staged one is kept
The staged change is committed and the unstaged one stays
The index entry is reset to HEAD; the working tree file is untouched
questions.explanation: --staged restores only the index, from HEAD by default. The working tree keeps its latest content, so both edits now appear as one unstaged modification ( M).

questions.text: In a project that has never been pushed anywhere, you run rm -rf .git. What is the result?
options: Git rebuilds .git from the working tree on the next git status
The current files stay, but all commits, branches and staged state are gone
Only the configuration is lost; history is stored with each file
The files are deleted too, because Git owns the working tree
questions.explanation: All history and metadata live inside .git. Removing it leaves plain files in a normal folder, and git status then fails with fatal: not a git repository.

questions.text: You run git clone https://github.com/djeada/git.git with no other arguments. Where does the working copy go?
options: Into the current directory, mixed in with any existing files
Into a new directory named git.git
Into a new directory named djeada/git
Into a new directory named git
questions.explanation: Without a destination, git clone uses the last path component of the URL and strips a trailing .git, so git.git becomes git.

questions.text: You run git clone <url> project, but project/ already exists and contains a file. What happens?
options: Clone aborts with fatal: destination path 'project' already exists and is not an empty directory.
Clone merges the remote files into the existing ones and keeps local copies on conflict
Clone overwrites the existing files with the versions from the remote
Clone creates project/project and places the repository inside it
questions.explanation: git clone accepts a destination only if it does not exist or is an empty directory. Anything else is refused with exit code 128.

questions.text: The remote has branches main and dev. Right after git clone, what does git branch (no options) list?
options: dev and main
Only * main
origin/dev and origin/main
Nothing until you run git fetch
questions.explanation: Clone creates remote-tracking branches for every remote branch (git branch -r shows origin/dev), but only one local branch: the remote's default. git switch dev creates a local dev from origin/dev.

questions.text: You are setting up a shared repository on a server that people will only push to and pull from. Which clone option fits?
options: --depth 1
--single-branch
--bare
--recurse-submodules
questions.explanation: A bare repository has no working tree, so there are no checked-out files to get out of sync when others push. Commands like git status in it fail with this operation must be run in a work tree.

questions.text: Your ~/.gitconfig sets user.email to me@personal.dev and the repository's .git/config sets it to me@work.com. Inside that repository, what does git config user.email print?
options: me@personal.dev, because global settings override local ones
Both addresses, one per line
An error, because the key is defined in two scopes
me@work.com, because local settings override global ones
questions.explanation: Git reads system, then global, then local config, and the last value read wins. Local therefore beats global, which beats system. git config --show-scope user.email confirms the value comes from local.

questions.text: Inside a repository you run git config user.email "ci@example.com" with no scope flag. Where is the value written?
options: .git/config of the current repository
~/.gitconfig
/etc/gitconfig
Nowhere, because a scope flag is required when writing
questions.explanation: Writing without a scope flag defaults to --local. Outside a repository the same command fails with fatal: not in a git directory.

questions.text: Commits in one repository keep getting an unexpected author email. Which command shows which config file the value comes from?
options: git config --get-all user.email
git config --global --list
git config --show-origin user.email
git log --format=%ae -1
questions.explanation: --show-origin prints the file path next to the value, for example file:.git/config. --get-all lists values without their source, and --global --list shows only one scope.

questions.text:
A directory contains app.log, important.log and notes.txt. With the .gitignore below, which files does git status --short list as untracked (besides .gitignore)?

*.log
!important.log
options: Only notes.txt
All three files
important.log and notes.txt
Only important.log
questions.explanation: *.log ignores every log file, then the later !important.log re-includes that one. Later matching patterns override earlier ones, so only app.log stays ignored.

questions.text:
With the .gitignore below, does build/keep.txt show up in git status?

build/
!build/keep.txt
options: Yes, because the negation comes after the directory rule
No, because Git cannot re-include a file whose parent directory is excluded
Yes, but only after running git add build/
No, because negation patterns are not allowed to contain a slash
questions.explanation: Once build/ is excluded, Git never looks inside it, so the negation has no effect. Write build/* instead to ignore the contents but still allow !build/keep.txt.

questions.text: The repository has a file TODO at the root and another at src/TODO. Which .gitignore line ignores only the root one?
options: TODO
TODO/
**/TODO
/TODO
questions.explanation: A leading slash anchors the pattern to the directory containing the .gitignore. A bare TODO or **/TODO matches at any depth, and TODO/ would match only directories.

questions.text: A root .gitignore contains src/*.txt. Which of these files is ignored?
options: src/c.txt
src/sub/c.txt
c.txt
docs/src/c.txt
questions.explanation: A pattern with a slash is relative to the .gitignore location, and * does not cross /. It matches only files directly in the top-level src/; src/**/*.txt would match nested ones too.

questions.text: config.env was committed weeks ago. You add config.env to .gitignore and then edit the file. What does git status --short show for it?
options: Nothing, because the file is now ignored
!! config.env
M config.env
D config.env
questions.explanation: .gitignore only affects untracked files. A file that is already in the index stays tracked, so its edits keep showing as modified until you remove it from the index.

questions.text: You want Git to stop tracking the already-committed config.env but keep the file on your disk. Which command do you run before committing?
options: git rm config.env
git restore --staged config.env
git reset --hard config.env
git rm --cached config.env
questions.explanation: --cached removes the file from the index only, so the next commit deletes it from the tree while the local copy remains. Plain git rm would also delete it from the working tree.

questions.text: app.log is matched by *.log in .gitignore. What happens when you run git add app.log?
options: Git refuses with exit code 1 and suggests -f to add it anyway
Git stages it silently, because naming a file overrides .gitignore
Git stages it and prints a warning, exiting with code 0
Git removes the matching line from .gitignore and stages the file
questions.explanation: Git prints The following paths are ignored by one of your .gitignore files and a hint to use -f. git add -f app.log stages it, after which the file is tracked like any other.

questions.text:
A .gitignore contains the single line below, and the directory has c.txt. Is c.txt ignored?

*.txt # text files
options: Yes, because everything after # is treated as a comment
No, because # starts a comment only at the beginning of a line
Yes, but only in the root directory
No, because patterns cannot contain spaces
questions.explanation: The whole line, including # text files, is one pattern, so it does not match c.txt. Put comments on their own lines.

questions.text: You want to ignore your editor's *.swp files in one repository without changing any file your teammates receive. Where do you add the pattern?
options: The repository's root .gitignore
A new .gitignore inside .git/
.git/info/exclude
.git/config under a [core] section
questions.explanation: .git/info/exclude uses .gitignore syntax but lives inside .git, so it is never committed or shared. A committed .gitignore would affect everyone.

questions.text: A file you expected to see in git status never appears. Which command tells you exactly which ignore file and line is hiding it?
options: git status --ignored
git check-ignore -v path/to/file
git ls-files --others
git config --get core.excludesFile
questions.explanation: git check-ignore -v prints the source file, line number and pattern, such as .gitignore:3:build/. git status --ignored shows ignored files (!!) but not which rule matched.

questions.text:
In a repository where a.txt is committed, you run the commands below. What does the last command print?

echo b >> a.txt
git add a.txt
echo c >> a.txt
git status --short
options: M a.txt
M a.txt
AM a.txt
MM a.txt
questions.explanation: The first column is index versus HEAD, the second is working tree versus index. The staged edit gives M in the first column and the later unstaged edit gives M in the second.

questions.text:
a.txt is tracked and unchanged. What does git status --short print after git rm --cached a.txt?

git rm --cached a.txt
git status --short
options: D a.txt
D a.txt followed by ?? a.txt
D a.txt only
Nothing, because the file is still on disk
questions.explanation: The index no longer has the file, so a deletion is staged (D in the first column). The file is still on disk and not ignored, so it also shows as untracked.

questions.text:
You rename a tracked file with the shell instead of Git. What does git status --short print?

mv old.txt new.txt
git status --short
options: D old.txt and ?? new.txt
R old.txt -> new.txt
R old.txt -> new.txt
D old.txt and A new.txt
questions.explanation: Nothing is staged yet, so Git sees an unstaged deletion and an untracked file. After git add -A the status becomes R old.txt -> new.txt, which is what git mv produces in one step.

questions.text: You edited the tracked app.py and created a new file util.py. What does git commit -am "Update" commit?
options: Both files, because -a means all files in the working tree
Nothing, because -a requires a prior git add
Only the change to app.py; util.py stays untracked
Only util.py, because new files take priority
questions.explanation: -a stages modifications and deletions of files Git already tracks. Untracked files must be added explicitly, so util.py still shows as ?? afterwards.

questions.text: You modified src/a, deleted top, and created src/new. Which describes the effect of git add -u at the repository root?
options: It stages all three changes
It stages only the new file src/new
It stages the modification only; deletions need git rm
It stages the modification and the deletion, but not src/new
questions.explanation: -u (update) works only on tracked files, so it records modifications and deletions. New files need git add <path>, git add ., or git add -A.

questions.text: You changed files in both src/ and docs/, then ran git add . from inside src/. What is staged?
options: Only the changes under src/
All changes in the repository
Only files directly in src/, not its subdirectories
Nothing, because git add . must be run at the root
questions.explanation: . is a pathspec for the current directory and everything below it. Changes in docs/ remain unstaged; git add -A without a path would stage the whole tree.

questions.text: You create a new directory assets/ containing two new files. What does git status --short show by default?
options: ?? assets/a.png and ?? assets/b.png
A assets/
?? assets/
Nothing, until the files are added
questions.explanation: By default status collapses a wholly untracked directory into one ?? line. git status --short -uall lists each file individually.

questions.text: You create an empty directory logs/ in a clean repository. What does git status --short print?
options: ?? logs/
Nothing
A logs/
!! logs/
questions.explanation: Git tracks file content, not directories, so an empty directory is invisible to it. Projects commonly add a placeholder file, such as .gitkeep, to keep the directory in the repository.

questions.text:
f.txt was committed containing one. You run the commands below. What does git diff --staged show as added?

echo two >> f.txt
git add f.txt
echo three >> f.txt
options: +three only
+two and +three
Nothing, because the file has unstaged changes
+two only
questions.explanation: git diff --staged (also --cached) compares the index with HEAD, which is exactly what the next commit will contain. Plain git diff compares the working tree with the index and would show only +three.

questions.text: In the same situation (two staged, three unstaged), which command shows both added lines in one diff?
options: git diff
git diff HEAD
git diff --staged
git status -v
questions.explanation: git diff HEAD compares the working tree with the last commit, so it includes staged and unstaged changes. git status -v shows only the staged diff unless given -v twice.

questions.text: You create a new file new.txt and edit the tracked f.txt, staging neither. What does git diff show?
options: The change to f.txt only
The changes to both files
The full content of new.txt only
Nothing, because nothing is staged
questions.explanation: git diff compares the working tree with the index, and an untracked file has no index entry to compare against. Once you git add new.txt, it appears in git diff --staged.

questions.text:
f.txt is committed as v1. What does cat f.txt print at the end?

echo v2 > f.txt
git add f.txt
echo v3 > f.txt
git restore f.txt
cat f.txt
options: v1
v3
v2
Nothing, because the file is deleted
questions.explanation: Without --source, git restore fills the working tree from the index, not from HEAD. The staged v2 comes back and v3 is lost; git status --short then shows M f.txt.

questions.text: f.txt is tracked and has unstaged edits. What happens when you run git rm f.txt?
options: Git refuses, reports local modifications, and suggests --cached or -f
Git deletes the file and stages the deletion, discarding the edits
Git stages the deletion but leaves the edited file on disk
Git commits the edits first and then removes the file
questions.explanation: git rm protects uncommitted work: it errors with the following file has local modifications and exits with 1. --cached keeps the file on disk and -f forces removal.

questions.text: You renamed top to top2 with git mv and committed. Which command lists the commits from before the rename as well?
options: git log -- top2
git log --all -- top2
git log --stat top2
git log --follow -- top2
questions.explanation: Git stores no rename record; it detects renames by comparing snapshots. --follow makes git log track a single file across renames, while a plain path filter stops at the rename commit.

questions.text: f.txt is clean. You run git restore --source=HEAD~1 f.txt. What does git status --short show next?
options: M f.txt, because the old version is staged
M f.txt, because only the working tree changed
Nothing, because HEAD moved back one commit
MM f.txt, because both index and working tree changed
questions.explanation: By default git restore writes only to the working tree, even with --source. HEAD and the index are untouched; add --staged to update the index as well.

questions.text: You commit, then notice you forgot to stage b.txt. You run git add b.txt and git commit --amend --no-edit. What is the result?
options: The last commit is replaced by a new commit, with a new hash, containing b.txt
A second commit containing only b.txt is added on top
The existing commit is modified in place and keeps its hash
The commit message is cleared because --no-edit skips the editor
questions.explanation: Commits are immutable, so amend creates a new commit with the same parent and replaces the branch tip. The commit count does not change, but the hash does, which matters if the old commit was pushed.

questions.text: You already pushed a commit to origin/main, then amended it locally. What does a plain git push do?
options: It replaces the remote commit, because the branch names match
It pushes the amended commit as a new commit after the old one
It succeeds and the remote keeps both versions on separate branches
It is rejected as non-fast-forward, because the histories have diverged
questions.explanation: The amended commit is not a descendant of the pushed one, and git status reports the branches have diverged. Replacing the remote commit requires a force push, ideally --force-with-lease.

questions.text: After amending a pushed commit, you push with --force-with-lease, but a teammate pushed a new commit since your last fetch. What happens?
options: The push succeeds and the teammate's commit is overwritten
The push is rejected as stale info, protecting the teammate's commit
Git automatically rebases your commit on top of the teammate's
The push succeeds and Git creates a merge commit on the remote
questions.explanation: --force-with-lease overwrites the remote branch only if it still points where your origin/main says it does. A plain --force would discard the teammate's commit.

questions.text: A bad commit is already on the shared main branch that teammates have pulled. What is the safest way to undo it?
options: git reset --hard HEAD~1 followed by git push --force
git commit --amend to empty the commit, then push
git restore --source=HEAD~1 . and push without committing
git revert <commit> and push the new commit
questions.explanation: git revert adds a new commit, such as Revert "Add c", that undoes the changes while keeping history intact. Resetting and force-pushing rewrites history that others already have.

questions.text: Your last commit modified a.txt and added b.txt. What does git status --short show after git reset --soft HEAD~1?
options: M a.txt and A b.txt
M a.txt and ?? b.txt
Nothing, because the changes are discarded
MM a.txt and AM b.txt
questions.explanation: --soft moves only the branch pointer; the index and working tree still hold the commit's content, so the changes appear staged and ready to recommit.

questions.text: With the same last commit (modified a.txt, added b.txt), what does git status --short show after git reset HEAD~1?
options: M a.txt and A b.txt
Nothing, because the changes are discarded
M a.txt and ?? b.txt
M a.txt and A b.txt
questions.explanation: With no mode flag, reset uses --mixed: it moves the branch and resets the index, but keeps the working tree. The changes become unstaged, and b.txt becomes untracked again.

questions.text: You have an edited tracked file and a new untracked file scratch.tmp. What remains after git reset --hard?
options: Both changes are gone and the directory matches HEAD exactly
Both changes remain, because no commit was given
The edit remains, but scratch.tmp is deleted
The edit is gone, but scratch.tmp is still there
questions.explanation: reset --hard resets the index and tracked files to HEAD, but never touches untracked files. Use git clean to remove those.

questions.text: You committed secret.txt, then ran git rm secret.txt and committed again. Can someone with a clone still read the secret?
options: No, because git rm removes the file from every commit
Only if they cloned before the second commit
Yes, for example with git show HEAD~1:secret.txt
No, because Git garbage-collects deleted files on the next push
questions.explanation: Deleting a file only affects the new snapshot; earlier commits still contain it. Removing it requires rewriting history with git filter-repo or git filter-branch, then rotating the leaked secret anyway.

questions.text: You strip secret.txt from main with git filter-branch --index-filter 'git rm -r --cached --ignore-unmatch secret.txt' HEAD. Why does git log --all --oneline -- secret.txt still list commits?
options: filter-branch saved the old history under refs/original/
--index-filter only rewrites the most recent commit
git log --all reads from the remote rather than local refs
The rewrite only takes effect after the next git commit
questions.explanation: filter-branch keeps a backup ref such as refs/original/refs/heads/main. Deleting it, expiring the reflog and running git gc --prune=now are needed before the old objects are really gone.

questions.text: Which command reliably reports whether any commit reachable from any ref still contains a file at the path secret.txt?
options: git grep "secret.txt" $(git rev-list --all)
git log --stat
git ls-files secret.txt
git log --all --oneline -- secret.txt
questions.explanation: A path filter with --all lists every commit, across all refs, that touched that path. git grep searches file contents for the text, not file names, and git log --stat only walks the current branch.

questions.text:
A merge stops on a conflict and the file contains the block below. Which text came from the branch you were on when you ran git merge feature?

<<<<<<< HEAD
mainv
=======
feat
>>>>>>> feature
options: feat, because the incoming branch is shown first
mainv, the part between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======
Neither; the block shows the common ancestor's versions
Both lines came from feature; HEAD marks the target position
questions.explanation: The section after <<<<<<< HEAD is your current branch's version, and the section before >>>>>>> feature is the incoming one. Edit the file, remove the markers, then git add it and commit.

questions.text: During that conflicted merge, what does git status --short show for the conflicted file f?
options: UU f
MM f
C f
!! f
questions.explanation: U marks an unmerged path, and UU means both sides modified it. After resolving, git add f clears the conflict state so the merge can be committed.

questions.text:
You are on main and run the commands below. Which branch is checked out afterwards?

git branch feature
git branch
options: main, because git branch feature only creates the branch
feature, because a new branch is checked out automatically
Neither, because HEAD is detached at the new branch's commit
feature, but only after the first commit is made on it
questions.explanation: git branch <name> creates a pointer at the current commit and leaves HEAD where it was, so git branch still marks main with the asterisk. Use git switch -c to create and switch in one step.

questions.text: Which single command creates a branch called login at the current commit and switches to it?
options: git branch -c login
git switch login
git switch -c login
git checkout login
questions.explanation: git switch -c (like git checkout -b) creates and checks out the branch. git switch login and git checkout login expect an existing branch, and git branch -c copies the current branch without switching to it.

questions.text:
You want to look at an old commit and run the command below. What happens?

git switch 1332864a242db6b0831408a94b979696ebfe313e
options: HEAD is detached at that commit and a warning is printed
A new branch named after the commit hash is created
The current branch is reset to point at that commit
It fails with fatal: a branch is expected, got commit
questions.explanation: git switch only switches to branches unless you pass --detach, so this fails with a hint to retry using git switch --detach <commit>. git checkout <commit> would detach HEAD without asking.

questions.text: You are on main. Branch feat has one commit that has not been merged anywhere. What does git branch -d feat do?
options: Deletes feat and prints a warning about the lost commit
Deletes feat and moves its commit onto main
Refuses with the branch 'feat' is not fully merged
Asks interactively whether to delete the unmerged commit
questions.explanation: -d is the safe delete: it exits with an error and keeps the branch when its commits are not merged. Only git branch -D feat (force) deletes it regardless.

questions.text:
You force-deleted a branch by mistake. How do you get it back?

$ git branch -D lost
Deleted branch lost (was 1cd5425).
options: git branch -u lost 1cd5425
git branch lost 1cd5425
git switch lost
git stash branch lost
questions.explanation: Deleting a branch removes only the name; the commit still exists until it is garbage-collected. Recreating a branch at the hash Git printed (or one found with git reflog) restores it. git switch lost fails because the name no longer exists.

questions.text: Branch feature has been merged into dev but not into main. You are on dev and feature has no upstream. What does git branch -d feature do?
options: Refuses, because -d only accepts branches merged into main
Refuses, because -d cannot delete a branch with no upstream
Deletes the branch and also removes its commits from dev
Deletes the branch, because its commits are reachable from HEAD
questions.explanation: Without an upstream, git branch -d checks whether the branch is merged into the current HEAD, not into main. Its commits stay in dev; only the branch name is removed.

questions.text: You are on main and run git branch -D main. What happens?
options: main is deleted and HEAD becomes detached at its last commit
Git refuses because main is the branch currently checked out
main is deleted and Git switches to the most recent other branch
main is deleted only if it is fully merged into its upstream
questions.explanation: Git will not delete the branch checked out in a worktree, even with -D; it reports cannot delete branch 'main' used by worktree. Switch to another branch first.

questions.text: In a fresh clone, git branch lists only main, but origin/feature exists. What does git switch feature do?
options: Creates a local feature branch that tracks origin/feature
Fails with invalid reference: feature because no local branch exists
Detaches HEAD at origin/feature so the remote branch can be inspected
Checks out origin/feature itself so new commits update the remote
questions.explanation: When exactly one remote has a matching branch, git switch <name> creates a local branch from it and sets up tracking (branch 'feature' set up to track 'origin/feature'). Remote-tracking branches themselves are never committed to directly.

questions.text:
You have unsaved edits in notes.txt and there is no branch called notes.txt. You meant to type a branch name. What do these two commands do?

git switch notes.txt
git checkout notes.txt
options: Both fail with invalid reference: notes.txt
Both discard your uncommitted edits to notes.txt
switch discards the edits; checkout fails with an error
switch fails with an error; checkout discards the edits
questions.explanation: git switch only handles branches, so it reports invalid reference. git checkout falls back to treating the argument as a path and silently restores the file from the index, losing the edits. That ambiguity is why switch and restore were added.

questions.text: You edited f on main, and f is different on branch other. What happens when you run git switch other?
options: Git switches and writes conflict markers into f
Git switches and your edit to f is discarded
Git refuses because your local changes would be overwritten
Git stashes your edit automatically before switching
questions.explanation: If a file you modified differs between the two branches, Git aborts with Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout. Uncommitted edits to files that are identical on both branches are simply carried across.

questions.text:
main has no new commits since feature was created. You run git merge feature on main and see the output below. What is true afterwards?

Updating b4ae40f..9b2bb65
Fast-forward
 g | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
options: A merge commit with two parents was added on top of main
The commits from feature were copied onto main with new hashes
feature was moved forward to match the tip of main
main now points at the same commit as feature
questions.explanation: A fast-forward just moves the main pointer forward to feature's tip; no new commit is created and no hashes change. Use --no-ff if you want a merge commit anyway.

questions.text:
main has commit A, and topic adds commit B on top of A. On main you run the commands below. What is printed?

git merge --no-ff --no-edit topic
git rev-list --count HEAD
options: 2
1
3
4
questions.explanation: A fast-forward was possible, but --no-ff forces a merge commit, so main now contains A, B and the merge commit M. Without --no-ff the count would be 2.

questions.text: main and side have diverged. What does git merge --ff-only side do on main?
options: Fails with Not possible to fast-forward, aborting and leaves main unchanged
Creates a merge commit, because a fast-forward is impossible here
Rebases main onto side so that the result is a fast-forward
Moves main to side, discarding the commit that only main had
questions.explanation: --ff-only merges only when main can simply move forward. With diverged history it aborts, and the hint suggests git merge --no-ff or git rebase instead.

questions.text:
You are on main, run git merge feature, and app.ini now looks like this. Which statement is correct?

<<<<<<< HEAD
color=green
=======
color=blue
>>>>>>> feature
options: color=green is from feature and color=blue is from main
color=green is the merge base and color=blue the merged result
color=green is from main and color=blue is from feature
color=green is the staged copy and color=blue the working copy
questions.explanation: The block after <<<<<<< HEAD is the version on the branch you are on (main), and the block before >>>>>>> feature is the incoming branch. Neither shows the merge base in the default conflict style.

questions.text: A merge stopped with a conflict in app.ini. What does git status --short show for that file?
options: MM app.ini
M app.ini
AA app.ini
UU app.ini
questions.explanation: UU means unmerged, both modified. AA is only used when both sides added the same new file, and M/MM appear once the file has been resolved and staged.

questions.text: During a conflicted merge you run git commit -m "merge" before resolving anything. What happens?
options: The merge commit is created with the conflict markers inside
It fails with Committing is not possible because you have unmerged files
The merge commit is created using the HEAD version of each file
Git aborts the merge and restores the pre-merge state
questions.explanation: Git will not commit while the index still has unmerged entries. You must edit the files, git add them to mark them resolved, then git commit or git merge --continue.

questions.text: A merge on main has produced conflicts you do not want to deal with now. Which command puts the branch back exactly as it was before the merge?
options: git merge --continue
git reset --soft HEAD
git stash
git merge --abort
questions.explanation: git merge --abort discards the merge in progress, removes MERGE_HEAD and restores the pre-merge files. git reset --soft is refused in the middle of a merge, and --continue requires the conflicts to be resolved first.

questions.text:
With merge.conflictStyle=diff3, a conflict looks like this. What is color=red?

<<<<<<< HEAD
color=green
||||||| dd36785
color=red
=======
color=blue
>>>>>>> feature
options: The version in the common ancestor (merge base)
The version currently staged in the index
The version Git suggests as the resolution
The version from the previous commit on feature
questions.explanation: The diff3 style adds a ||||||| section showing the merge base. Seeing the original line makes it clear that both branches changed red, one to green and one to blue.

questions.text: During a merge you run git add app.ini while the file still contains <<<<<<< markers, then git commit --no-edit. What happens?
options: git add refuses to stage a file that contains markers
The commit succeeds and the markers are committed
git commit refuses because markers are still present
Git strips the markers and keeps the HEAD version
questions.explanation: Git treats git add as "this file is resolved" and does not inspect the content, so the merge commit records the markers. Always check the file (or git diff --check) before staging.

questions.text: On feature (commits F1 and F2), you run git rebase main after main gained commit M1. It succeeds. Which statement is true?
options: F1 and F2 are replaced by new commits with different hashes
F1 and F2 keep their hashes; only their parent pointer is updated
A merge commit joining main into feature is created
main is moved forward to include F1 and F2
questions.explanation: Rebase replays each commit on top of main, creating new commits because a commit's hash covers its parent. The old tip is still available as ORIG_HEAD or in the reflog; main itself does not move.

questions.text: You rebased feature onto main without conflicts. What happens when you then run git merge feature on main?
options: A fast-forward, because feature now sits directly on top of main
A merge commit, because rebased branches always need a merge commit
A conflict, because the rebased commits duplicate commits on main
Nothing, because the rebase already added the commits to main
questions.explanation: After the rebase, main's tip is an ancestor of feature, so the merge just moves main forward. This is why rebasing before merging gives a linear history.

questions.text: On feature you run git rebase main and it stops with a conflict in f. main has mainline in f; your feature commit has feat. What does f contain after git checkout --ours f?
options: feat, because "ours" is always the branch you started on
mainline, because during a rebase "ours" is the branch being rebuilt on
The merge-base content, because "ours" means the common ancestor
The file with conflict markers, because --ours only works for merges
questions.explanation: A rebase checks out main and replays your commits onto it, so HEAD ("ours") is the main side and "theirs" is the commit being replayed. This is the reverse of what happens in a merge.

questions.text: A rebase of feature stopped with a conflict and you decide to give up. Which command returns feature to exactly the commits it had before the rebase?
options: git rebase --skip
git merge --abort
git rebase --continue
git rebase --abort
questions.explanation: git rebase --abort stops the rebase and resets the branch to its original tip. --skip drops the conflicting commit and continues, and git merge --abort fails because no merge is in progress.

questions.text: You run cat .git/HEAD first while on main, then again after git switch --detach HEAD~1. What do you see?
options: ref: refs/heads/main, then a raw 40-character commit hash
A raw 40-character commit hash both times
ref: refs/heads/main both times
ref: refs/heads/main, then ref: refs/heads/HEAD~1
questions.explanation: Normally HEAD is a symbolic reference to a branch. When detached, .git/HEAD holds the commit hash directly, which is why new commits there are not recorded on any branch.

questions.text:
In a CI job that checked out a commit in detached HEAD state, what do these commands print?

git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD
git branch --show-current
options: The commit hash, then the commit hash
main, then main
An error, then an error
HEAD, then an empty line
questions.explanation: With no branch checked out, rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD falls back to the literal HEAD, and branch --show-current prints nothing. Scripts that read the branch name this way need to handle both cases.

questions.text:
While detached you made a commit, then ran git switch main. Git warned you were leaving one commit behind. How do you save it?

$ git reflog -3
31d66d4 HEAD@{0}: checkout: moving from 1e9a71a9d56c499ecc094ec3446b465011df3367 to main
1e9a71a HEAD@{1}: commit: detached work
60158eb HEAD@{2}: checkout: moving from main to HEAD~1
options: git switch 1e9a71a
git branch rescue 1e9a71a
git reset --hard HEAD@{0}
git stash pop
questions.explanation: The reflog still records the detached commit, so creating a branch at 1e9a71a gives it a permanent name. git switch <hash> fails without --detach, and HEAD@{0} is the current commit, so that reset does nothing.

questions.text: You are in detached HEAD state and have made two commits you want to keep. Which command keeps them on a new branch?
options: git switch keep
git checkout -b keep main
git switch -c keep
git branch keep main
questions.explanation: git switch -c keep creates the branch at the current (detached) commit and attaches HEAD to it. Giving main as the start point would create a branch that does not contain the two commits.

questions.text:
HEAD is the merge commit M below. Which commit does HEAD^2 refer to?

*   M  (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'side'
|\
| * S  (side) side
* | P  main2
|/
* B  feat1
* A  base
options: P
B
S
A
questions.explanation: ^2 selects the second parent of a merge commit, which is the branch that was merged in (S). HEAD^ or HEAD^1 would be the first parent, P.

questions.text:
Using the same history, which commit does HEAD~2 refer to?

*   M  (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'side'
|\
| * S  (side) side
* | P  main2
|/
* B  feat1
* A  base
options: S
B
P
A
questions.explanation: ~2 follows the first parent twice: M to P, then P to B. It is the same as HEAD^^, and it never goes through the second parent the way HEAD^2 does.

questions.text:
You commit B on top of A, then run git reset --hard HEAD~1. What does the last command print?

git log -1 --format=%s HEAD@{1}
options: A
Nothing, because the reset deleted B
fatal: ambiguous argument 'HEAD@{1}'
B
questions.explanation: HEAD@{1} means where HEAD was one move ago in the reflog, which was B before the reset. This differs from HEAD~1, the parent of the current commit.

questions.text: feature branched from base and has F1, F2, F3; main has since gained M1 and M2. Which commits does git log --oneline main..feature list?
options: M2, M1
F3, F2, F1, base
All five of F1–F3 and M1–M2
questions.explanation: A..B lists commits reachable from B but not from A, so it shows what feature has that main lacks. Swapping the order (feature..main) would list M2 and M1.

questions.text: With the same history (F1–F3 only on feature, M1–M2 only on main), what does git rev-list --count main...feature print?
options: 3
2
5
6
questions.explanation: For log-style commands, A...B is the symmetric difference: commits reachable from either side but not both, here F1–F3 plus M1–M2. Add --left-right to see which side each commit is on.

questions.text: You want to review only the changes feature made since it branched off, ignoring what landed on main meanwhile. Which command shows that?
options: git diff main..feature
git diff main...feature
git diff feature..main
git diff feature main
questions.explanation: For git diff, main...feature compares the merge base with feature. The two-dot form compares the two tips directly, so main's new changes appear as reversed edits.

questions.text:
You created light with git tag light and v1.0 with git tag -a v1.0 -m "Release 1.0". What do these commands print?

git cat-file -t light
git cat-file -t v1.0
options: commit, then tag
tag, then tag
tag, then commit
commit, then commit
questions.explanation: A lightweight tag is just a ref pointing straight at a commit. An annotated tag creates a separate tag object holding the tagger, date and message, which then points at the commit.

questions.text: A teammate says git show v2.0 displays the commit but no Tagger: line and no tag message. What is the most likely reason?
options: v2.0 is a lightweight tag, which has no tag object
The tag was created locally and has not been pushed yet
git show needs --tags to display tag metadata
The tag points to a merge commit, which hides the message
questions.explanation: Only annotated tags (git tag -a) store a tagger, date and message, which git show prints before the commit. A lightweight tag is just a name for the commit, so only the commit is shown.

questions.text: You tag a release with git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "v1.2.0" and then run git push origin main. What does the remote have?
options: The updated main and the v1.2.0 tag
The updated main but no v1.2.0 tag
The v1.2.0 tag but not the updated main
Neither, because the tag blocks the push
questions.explanation: Pushing a branch does not push tags. Push the tag explicitly with git push origin v1.2.0, all tags with git push origin --tags, or annotated ones automatically with --follow-tags.

questions.text: HEAD has a lightweight tag light2 and an annotated tag v2. Neither is on the remote. Which tags does git push --follow-tags origin main send?
options: Only v2
Only light2
Both v2 and light2
Neither of them
questions.explanation: --follow-tags pushes annotated tags that point at commits being pushed, but ignores lightweight tags. That is why release tags should be annotated.

questions.text: You need to publish every local tag, including lightweight ones, to origin. Which command does that?
options: git push --all origin
git push --follow-tags origin main
git push origin --tags
git push origin main
questions.explanation: --tags pushes all refs under refs/tags, of either kind. --all pushes all branches but no tags, and --follow-tags skips lightweight tags.

questions.text: Tag light is already on the remote. You move it locally with git tag -f light HEAD and run git push origin light. What happens?
options: The remote tag is updated to the new commit
A second tag light is added beside the old one
The remote tag is deleted and must be pushed again
The push is rejected because the tag already exists
questions.explanation: Git refuses to overwrite an existing tag on the remote (! [rejected] light -> light (already exists)). Forcing it with git push -f origin light works, but moving a published tag breaks anyone who already fetched it.

questions.text: The only tag in your history is a lightweight tag v0.9, one commit behind HEAD. What does plain git describe do?
options: Prints v0.9-1-g<hash>
Fails with No annotated tags can describe
Prints v0.9
Prints only the abbreviated commit hash
questions.explanation: By default git describe only considers annotated tags. It suggests --tags, which would print v0.9-1-g<hash> (tag, commits since tag, abbreviated hash).

questions.text: A bug was found in release v1.2.0. You want to start a fix from exactly that release on a new branch. Which command does it?
options: git switch -c hotfix v1.2.0
git switch v1.2.0
git branch hotfix
git checkout v1.2.0 hotfix
questions.explanation: git switch -c <branch> <start-point> creates a branch at the tagged commit and switches to it. git switch v1.2.0 fails without --detach, and git branch hotfix starts at the current HEAD instead of the tag.

questions.text: You modified the tracked file app.js and created a new file untracked.txt. After git stash, what does git status --short show?
options: ?? untracked.txt
M app.js
Nothing, because the working tree is clean
A untracked.txt
questions.explanation: Plain git stash saves tracked changes (staged and unstaged) and leaves untracked files where they are. Use git stash -u to include them.

questions.text: You edited app.js and created an untracked config.local. build/ is in .gitignore. You want to stash app.js and config.local but leave build/ alone. Which command?
options: git stash -a
git stash -u
git stash
git stash --keep-index
questions.explanation: -u (--include-untracked) adds untracked files to the stash but skips ignored ones. -a (--all) would also stash the ignored build/ directory, and plain git stash would leave config.local behind.

questions.text: On main you run git stash push -m "wip login". What line does git stash list show for it?
options: stash@{0}: WIP on main: wip login
stash@{0}: WIP on main: 687b321 wip login
stash@{0}: On main: 687b321 Initial commit
stash@{0}: On main: wip login
questions.explanation: A stash with a message is listed as On <branch>: <message>. Without -m, Git uses WIP on <branch>: <hash> <commit subject> instead.

questions.text: You have one stash entry and run git stash apply. It applies cleanly. What does git stash list show now?
options: Nothing, because applying a stash removes it
The same stash@{0} entry as before
The entry renamed to stash@{1}
The entry marked as applied
questions.explanation: apply restores the changes but keeps the stash entry, so you can apply it elsewhere too. git stash pop is apply followed by drop, and git stash drop removes an entry on its own.

questions.text: You run git stash pop and it reports a conflict in app.js. What happened to the stash entry?
options: It was dropped, so the conflicted file is the only copy left
It was moved to a new branch named after the stash
It was kept, and Git says so in its output
It was split into a resolved and an unresolved part
questions.explanation: When pop hits a conflict, Git prints The stash entry is kept in case you need it again. After resolving, run git stash drop yourself.

questions.text:
Before stashing, git status --short showed the output below. After git stash and then git stash apply (no flags), what does it show?

M  app.js
 M lib.js
A  new.js
options: M app.js, M lib.js, A new.js
M app.js, M lib.js, A new.js
M app.js, M lib.js, ?? new.js
M app.js, M lib.js, A new.js
questions.explanation: Without --index, apply restores modifications to the working tree only, so the staged change to app.js comes back unstaged. A newly added file stays added. git stash apply --index would restore the original staging exactly.

questions.text: You have an uncommitted edit to app.js, and the newest stash also changes app.js. What does git stash apply do?
options: Merges both edits and marks conflicting lines with markers
Overwrites your edit with the stashed version of app.js
Refuses because your local changes would be overwritten
Applies the stash and drops it, keeping both edits
questions.explanation: Git will not merge a stash into uncommitted changes to the same file; it aborts with Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge and the stash stays. Commit or stash your edit first.

questions.text: You stashed work on main, then main moved on and popping now conflicts. What does git stash branch fix stash@{0} do?
options: Creates fix at the current tip of main, applies the stash and keeps it
Creates fix from the stash's changes but stays on main
Commits the stash onto a new branch fix without touching your files
Creates fix at the commit the stash was made on, applies it, then drops it
questions.explanation: Starting from the original commit means the stash applies without conflicts. Git switches to fix, applies the changes and prints Dropped stash@{0} when it succeeds.

questions.text:
You stash some work on main, then switch to other and run git stash list. What do you see?

$ git stash -q
$ git switch -q other
$ git stash list
options: Nothing, because stashes are stored per branch
An error, because the stash belongs to main
stash@{0}: WIP on main: f59a74e init
stash@{0}: WIP on other: f59a74e init
questions.explanation: There is one stash list for the whole repository; the entry only records which branch it came from. You can apply it on other, which is a common way to move uncommitted work between branches.

questions.text:
You run the commands below. What change does the last command show for f?

echo v1 > f && git add f && git commit -qm one
echo v2 > f && git add f
echo v3 > f
git diff --cached
options: v2 replaced by v3
v1 replaced by v2
v1 replaced by v3
No output, because f also has unstaged changes
questions.explanation: git diff --cached compares the index (v2) with HEAD (v1). Plain git diff would show v2 to v3, and git diff HEAD would show v1 to v3.

questions.text: You edited the tracked file app.js and created a new file notes.txt that you have not added. What does git diff HEAD show?
options: The changes to app.js only, because untracked files never appear in a diff
Both files, because it compares the whole working directory with HEAD
Only notes.txt, because tracked changes need git diff --cached
Nothing, until notes.txt is either staged or ignored
questions.explanation: git diff and its variants only compare tracked content. An untracked file shows up in git status, but it appears in a diff only after you stage it (or mark it with git add -N).

questions.text: feature branched off main, and both branches have new commits since then. What does git log main..feature list?
options: Commits on main that are not on feature
Commits on either branch but not on both
Commits reachable from feature that are not reachable from main
Every commit between the two branch tips in date order
questions.explanation: A..B means "reachable from B, excluding anything reachable from A", so it lists what feature would add to main. The symmetric "either but not both" set is main...feature.

questions.text: Since branching, main added file h and feature added file g. Which files appear in git diff --stat main...feature?
options: g and h, with h shown as deleted
Only h, shown as deleted
g and h, both shown as added
Only g
questions.explanation: With three dots, git diff compares the merge base with feature, so you see only what feature changed. Two dots (or a space) compares the two tips, which makes h look deleted.

questions.text: The line timeout = 30 was added to a file in commit c2, an unrelated line was added in c3, and the timeout line was deleted in c4. Which commits does git log --oneline -S 'timeout' list?
options: Only c2, the commit that added the string
c2 and c4
c2, c3 and c4, since the file contained the string in all of them
Only c4, the most recent commit that touched it
questions.explanation: The pickaxe -S lists commits that change how many times the string occurs, so both adding and removing it count. c3 left the count unchanged, so it is not listed.

questions.text: What does git show HEAD~2:config.yml do?
options: Prints config.yml as it was two commits before HEAD, leaving the working tree alone
Restores config.yml from two commits ago into the working tree
Shows the diff that commit HEAD~2 made to config.yml
Checks out HEAD~2 as a detached HEAD and opens the file
questions.explanation: The <commit>:<path> syntax names the file's blob in that commit, and git show prints its contents. Nothing is checked out or restored; use git restore --source to actually bring the old version back.

questions.text: Which command shows, for each of lines 10 to 20 of app.js, the commit and author that last changed it?
options: git log -p -- app.js
git show -L 10,20 app.js
git blame -L 10,20 app.js
git diff HEAD -- app.js
questions.explanation: git blame annotates each line with the last commit, author and date that touched it, and -L limits it to a line range. git log -p shows whole commits, not per-line attribution.

questions.text: Alice wrote the logic in f.py; later Bob reindented every line. git blame f.py now shows Bob on every line. Why?
options: git blame always shows the most recent committer of the file as a whole
git blame reports the last commit that changed each line, and the reindent changed every line
git blame shows whoever last ran git add on the file
git blame attributes lines to the person who merged them into main
questions.explanation: Blame is per line and per last change, so a whitespace-only commit takes over every line it touched. git blame -w ignores whitespace changes and shows Alice again.

questions.text: You know tag v1.0 was good and the current HEAD is bad. Which sequence correctly starts a bisect session?
options: git bisect start v1.0 HEAD
git bisect start, git bisect good HEAD, git bisect bad v1.0
git bisect start, git bisect bad, git bisect good v1.0
git bisect run v1.0..HEAD
questions.explanation: git bisect bad without an argument marks the current commit. git bisect start takes the bad commit first, so start v1.0 HEAD swaps them and Git complains that the good rev is not an ancestor of the bad one.

questions.text: During git bisect run ./test.sh, the script exits with code 125 on a commit that does not compile. What does bisect do with that commit?
options: Marks it bad, like any non-zero exit code
Aborts the whole bisect session
Marks it good, because 125 means success with warnings
Skips it and tests a nearby commit instead
questions.explanation: For bisect run, exit 0 marks a commit good, other small codes such as 1 mark it bad, and 125 is reserved for "cannot test this commit", which works like git bisect skip.

questions.text: You rebased feature onto main and want to see where feature pointed just before the rebase. Which reference names that commit?
options: HEAD@{1}
feature@{1}
HEAD~1
feature~1
questions.explanation: The branch reflog records the whole rebase as one update, so feature@{1} is the old tip (as is ORIG_HEAD). HEAD@{1} points at the last picked commit, because HEAD moved once per replayed commit.

questions.text: A teammate pushed a commit to main on origin a minute ago. You have not run any network command since. What does git log origin/main show you?
options: The new commit, because origin/main always reflects the server
An error, because origin/main can only be read after git pull
main as it was on origin when you last fetched or pushed, without the new commit
Your local main, because origin/main is just another name for it
questions.explanation: origin/main is a remote-tracking branch: a local record of the server's branch, updated only by fetch, pull or push. That is also why git status can say "up to date" while the server has moved on.

questions.text: You run git checkout origin/main and then make a commit. What happens?
options: HEAD is detached at that commit; the new commit moves only HEAD, not origin/main
The commit is added to origin/main and goes to the server on the next git push
Git creates a local main tracking origin/main and commits there
Git refuses, because remote-tracking branches cannot be checked out
questions.explanation: Checking out a remote-tracking branch detaches HEAD; only fetches and pushes move origin/main. git switch origin/main refuses outright, and git switch main is what creates a tracking local branch.

questions.text: After git fetch origin, which of these has changed?
options: Your current branch, fast-forwarded if possible
Your working tree, but not the index
Your local branches and their remote-tracking branches, but not the working tree
Only remote-tracking branches such as origin/main, plus the downloaded objects
questions.explanation: Fetch downloads objects and updates refs/remotes/origin/*. Your branches, index and files stay as they were until you merge, rebase or reset.

questions.text: Your main and origin/main have diverged, and pull.rebase is not configured. With Git 2.43 you run plain git pull. What happens?
options: Git creates a merge commit, because merge is the default
Git fetches, then stops and asks you to choose merge, rebase or fast-forward only
Git rebases your local commits on top of origin/main
Git aborts before fetching and leaves origin/main unchanged
questions.explanation: The fetch half runs and updates origin/main, then Git fails with fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches. You pick with --rebase, --no-rebase, --ff-only or the pull.rebase setting.

questions.text: You have one unpushed commit and origin/main has one commit you do not have. After git pull --rebase, what does the first line of git status -sb show?
options: ## main...origin/main [ahead 1, behind 1]
## main...origin/main [ahead 2]
## main...origin/main [ahead 1]
## main...origin/main
questions.explanation: The rebase replays your commit (with a new hash) on top of the fetched one, so you are no longer behind and are one commit ahead, ready to push as a fast-forward.

questions.text:
git push prints the output below. What is the right next step?

 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'https://example.com/team/app.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not
hint: have locally.
options: Run git push --force so the remote matches your branch
Run git push -u origin main to fix the missing upstream
Run git fetch --prune, then push again unchanged
Integrate the remote commits with git pull (merge or rebase), then push
questions.explanation: The server's branch has commits that your push would throw away, so it is not a fast-forward. Integrate them first; forcing would delete a teammate's work.

questions.text: You amend a commit that you already pushed, then run git push. It is rejected as (non-fast-forward). Why?
options: The remote rejects any commit whose message has changed
The new commit does not build on the old remote tip, so it is not a fast-forward
You must run git push -u again after amending to re-link the upstream
The remote already has a commit with the same message and refuses the duplicate
questions.explanation: Amending creates a new commit that replaces the old one instead of building on it. Publishing it requires a force push, which is why you should not amend commits others may have pulled.

questions.text: On a new local branch topic, git push fails with fatal: The current branch topic has no upstream branch. Which command pushes and sets up tracking in one step?
options: git branch -u origin/topic, then git push
git push --force origin topic
git push -u origin topic
git fetch origin topic, then git push
questions.explanation: -u (--set-upstream) creates topic on the remote and records origin/topic as its upstream. git branch -u origin/topic fails first, because origin/topic does not exist until something is pushed.

questions.text: git branch -vv shows * topic c87ab1c [origin/topic: ahead 2] Add parser. What does ahead 2 mean?
options: topic has 2 commits that origin/topic, as last fetched, does not have
origin/topic has 2 commits that you have not merged yet
The server's topic is 2 commits ahead of what you last fetched
2 commits on topic failed to push and must be retried
questions.explanation: Ahead/behind counts compare your branch with its local remote-tracking branch, so they show unpushed and unmerged commits as of your last fetch, not live server state.

questions.text: You rewrote feature locally. Meanwhile a teammate pushed a new commit to origin/feature, and you have not fetched. What does git push --force-with-lease do?
options: It overwrites the teammate's commit, just like --force
It merges the teammate's commit into yours, then pushes
It pushes your branch and keeps the teammate's commit as a separate branch
It is rejected as (stale info), and the teammate's commit stays
questions.explanation: By default the lease expects the server's branch to still match your origin/feature, and here it does not. Plain --force has no such check and would silently overwrite the teammate's commit.

questions.text: Same situation, but your editor ran git fetch in the background before you pushed, and you did not look at the new commit. What does git push --force-with-lease do now?
options: It is rejected, because the lease remembers the value from before the fetch
It succeeds and discards the teammate's commit, because origin/feature now matches the server
It is rejected, because --force-with-lease refuses whenever the remote has commits you lack
It succeeds, but the server keeps the teammate's commit on a backup branch
questions.explanation: The lease only compares the server with your remote-tracking ref, and the fetch updated it. Check git log HEAD..origin/feature before pushing, or pass an explicit expected value with --force-with-lease=feature:<sha>.

questions.text: A force push to a bare server repository overwrote a commit you need. Where are you most likely to find that commit's hash?
options: In the server's reflog, which records every push by default
In git log origin/feature, which still shows the old tip
In git reflog show origin/feature in a clone that had fetched the old tip
Nowhere, because a force push deletes the commit from every clone
questions.explanation: Bare repositories keep no reflog by default, but each clone records every past value of its remote-tracking branches. A teammate's local branch may also still contain the commit.

questions.text: A teammate deleted topic on the server. You had a local topic tracking it. What does git fetch --prune do?
options: Deletes origin/topic; local topic stays and git branch -vv shows [origin/topic: gone]
Deletes both origin/topic and your local topic
Deletes local topic only if it is fully merged into main
Changes nothing until you also run git remote prune origin
questions.explanation: Pruning removes stale remote-tracking refs only; Git never deletes your local branches for you. Without --prune or fetch.prune=true, a plain git fetch would keep origin/topic as well.

questions.text: You want your local main to match origin's main exactly, discarding your two local commits and uncommitted changes to tracked files. Which commands do that?
options: git fetch then git reset --soft origin/main
git fetch then git reset --hard origin/main
git fetch then git checkout origin/main
git pull --force
questions.explanation: reset --hard moves main to origin/main and overwrites the index and tracked files. --soft would keep the discarded changes staged, and checking out origin/main only detaches HEAD.

questions.text: You forked a project and cloned your fork as origin. How do you bring the original project's new commits into your local main?
options: git pull origin main
git push upstream main
git fetch --all then git merge origin/main
git remote add upstream <url>, git fetch upstream, then git merge upstream/main
questions.explanation: Your fork does not receive the original project's commits automatically, so pulling from origin gets nothing new. Add the original as a second remote, fetch it, and merge its main.

questions.text: You run git rebase -i HEAD~4. Which commit is on the first line of the todo list?
options: HEAD, the newest commit
HEAD~4, the base you passed
HEAD~3, the oldest of the four commits being rewritten
The first commit of the repository
questions.explanation: The todo list runs top to bottom in the order commits will be replayed, so the oldest comes first. HEAD~4 itself is the base and is not rewritten.

questions.text: You change the todo list to pick A, fixup B, fixup C and save. What is the result?
options: One commit with all three changes and only A's message, with no message editor opened
One commit with all three changes, after an editor opens pre-filled with all three messages
Three commits, with B's and C's messages removed
One commit with only A's changes; B and C are dropped
questions.explanation: fixup melds a commit into the one above it and discards its message, so no editor is needed. squash would open an editor with the combined messages.

questions.text: In a git rebase -i HEAD~3 todo list you change the first line from pick to squash. What happens?
options: Git squashes that commit into its parent, HEAD~3
Git stops with cannot 'squash' without a previous commit
Git silently treats the first squash as pick
Git squashes that commit into the commit on the next line
questions.explanation: squash and fixup combine a commit with the one before it in the list, and the first line has none. The base commit is outside the list; widen the range if you want to fold into it.

questions.text: In an interactive rebase todo list you delete the whole line for one commit, then save. What happens to that commit?
options: It is kept, because missing lines default to pick
Git aborts the rebase because the todo list is incomplete
Its changes are squashed into the previous commit
It is dropped from the rewritten branch
questions.explanation: Removing a line has the same effect as drop. The original commit is still reachable from the reflog if you change your mind.

questions.text: You run git commit --fixup a1b2c3d and later git rebase -i --autosquash main. What does the todo list look like?
options: The fixup! commit stays last in the list, marked pick
The fixup! commit is listed first, so it applies before its target
The fixup! commit is moved directly below a1b2c3d and marked fixup
The fixup! commit is left out, and its changes are applied after the rebase
questions.explanation: --fixup writes a fixup! <subject> message, and --autosquash uses it to reorder and mark the line. Set rebase.autoSquash=true to make this the default for rebase -i.

questions.text: feature has 4 commits since it branched from main. On feature you run git reset --soft $(git merge-base main HEAD). What is the state now?
options: feature points at the fork point, and the changes from all 4 commits are staged
feature points at main's tip, and the changes are unstaged
The 4 commits are deleted together with their changes
feature is unchanged; only the index is reset to the fork point
questions.explanation: --soft moves only the branch pointer and keeps the index and working tree, so a single git commit -m "..." now records the whole feature as one commit.

questions.text: Right after that reset --soft, you run git commit --amend -m "feat: search" instead of a plain commit. What happens?
options: It amends the last of the 4 feature commits, as intended
Git refuses, because there is nothing to amend after a reset
It creates a new commit on top of the fork point
It rewrites main's fork-point commit into a new commit on feature
questions.explanation: After the reset, HEAD is the merge base, a commit that belongs to main. --amend replaces it with a new commit that also contains its changes. A plain git commit is what you want.

questions.text: You run git merge --squash feat on main, then git commit. Afterwards git branch -d feat fails with "not fully merged". Why?
options: The squash merge left unresolved conflicts behind on feat
The squash commit has a single parent, so feat's commits are not reachable from main
git branch -d never deletes a branch that has been pushed
merge --squash locks the source branch until you run git merge --continue
questions.explanation: A squash merge copies the combined changes into one ordinary commit and records no merge, so Git cannot see that feat is merged. Use git branch -D feat once you are sure.

questions.text: You run git merge --squash feat on main. What state are you in before you commit?
options: A new commit exists on main with a message listing every feat commit
A merge commit with two parents exists, holding one combined diff
The combined changes from feat are staged, and no commit has been created yet
Only the changes from feat's last commit have been applied
questions.explanation: --squash updates the index and working tree but stops before committing and does not set MERGE_HEAD. Your next git commit creates one regular commit.

questions.text: README has uncommitted edits and untracked.txt is untracked. You run git archive -o out.zip HEAD. What does out.zip contain?
options: The committed README and no untracked.txt
Your edited README and untracked.txt
Your edited README but no untracked.txt
The committed README plus untracked.txt, since it is in the same folder
questions.explanation: git archive packs the tree of the commit you name, not the working directory, so uncommitted edits and untracked files are never included.

questions.text: You add secret.txt export-ignore to .gitattributes but do not commit it. git archive HEAD still includes secret.txt. Why?
options: export-ignore only works with --format=zip
git archive reads attributes from the tree being archived, and HEAD has no such rule
Archive exclusions must be listed in .gitignore instead
secret.txt must also be untracked for the rule to apply
questions.explanation: Commit the .gitattributes change, or pass --worktree-attributes to use the working copy's attributes. .gitignore has no effect on files that are already tracked.

questions.text: What paths does git archive --prefix=proj HEAD README | tar -t list?
options: proj/README
README, because --prefix only applies with -o
projREADME
proj/ and proj/README
questions.explanation: The prefix is prepended as a literal string, so you need the trailing slash. --prefix=proj/ produces proj/ and proj/README.

questions.text: Your repository contains a submodule at libs/sub. What does git archive HEAD put at that path?
options: An empty libs/sub/ directory
The submodule's files at the commit recorded in HEAD
The submodule's files at its latest upstream commit
A text file containing the submodule's commit hash
questions.explanation: The superproject only stores a gitlink (a commit hash) for the submodule, and git archive does not recurse into it. Package submodules separately.

questions.text: You committed too early and want to undo the last commit but keep its changes staged, ready to recommit. Which command?
options: git reset --hard HEAD~1
git reset HEAD~1
git revert HEAD
git reset --soft HEAD~1
questions.explanation: --soft moves the branch back and leaves the index alone. The default --mixed would also unstage the changes, --hard would discard them, and revert adds a new undo commit.

questions.text: The last commit modified tracked file f. You run git reset HEAD~1 with no mode flag. What does git status --short show?
options: M f
M f
?? f
Nothing; the change is gone
questions.explanation: The default --mixed mode resets the branch and the index but not the working tree, so the change is still in f but unstaged (M in the second column).

questions.text: You have an uncommitted edit to tracked file f and a new untracked file untracked.txt. You run git reset --hard HEAD~1. What does git status --short show?
options: Nothing; --hard wipes tracked and untracked changes
M f and ?? untracked.txt
?? untracked.txt only
M f and ?? untracked.txt
questions.explanation: reset --hard overwrites the index and tracked files but never touches untracked files. Removing those is the job of git clean.

questions.text: The working tree has untracked untracked.txt, untracked directory build/, and debug.log, which matches .gitignore. What does git clean -fd remove?
options: build/ and untracked.txt; the ignored debug.log stays
Only untracked.txt; directories also need -x
All three, because -d includes ignored files
Nothing, until you confirm each file interactively
questions.explanation: -f is required to delete anything and -d adds untracked directories. Ignored files are removed only with -x. Run git clean -nd first to preview.

questions.text: You force-deleted an unmerged branch and Git printed Deleted branch exp (was 5e14eed). How do you get the branch back?
options: git reset --hard exp@{1}
git branch exp 5e14eed
git revert 5e14eed
git switch exp, since deletion only hides the branch
questions.explanation: Deleting a branch removes only the ref (and its own reflog); the commits remain until garbage collection. Recreate the ref at the printed hash, or find it in git reflog if it has scrolled away.

questions.text: You meant to undo one commit but ran git reset --hard HEAD~3. Nothing else has happened since. What restores the branch to where it was?
options: git revert HEAD~3..HEAD
git restore --source=HEAD~3 .
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
git pull, which re-downloads the missing commits
questions.explanation: HEAD@{1} is where HEAD was before its last move, so resetting to it undoes the reset (ORIG_HEAD works too). The commits were never deleted, just unreferenced.

questions.text: You clone a repository fresh and immediately run git reflog. What does it show?
options: The HEAD history of every developer who has pushed to the repository
The server's reflog for the default branch
Nothing, because reflogs must first be enabled in config
A single clone: from ... entry
questions.explanation: Reflogs are local and are never pushed or cloned. Your reflog only records movements in your own repository, so it cannot recover a teammate's unpushed work.

questions.text: History is A-B-C-D-E, and secret.txt was added in C along with other changes. You run git filter-repo --invert-paths --path secret.txt. Which commits get new hashes?
options: Every commit, A through E
Commits from C onward; A and B keep their hashes
Only C; D and E keep theirs
None; only the secret.txt blob is removed from storage
questions.explanation: A commit's hash covers its tree and its parent, so changing C changes every descendant. Commits before C have identical content and keep their IDs. Rotate the secret anyway, since old clones still contain it.

questions.text: You rebased the shared branch feature and force-pushed. A teammate who had the old commits and nothing new runs git fetch then git status. What do they see?
options: Their feature has diverged from origin/feature, with the old commits counted as ahead
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/feature'
Your branch is behind 'origin/feature' and can be fast-forwarded
An error saying origin/feature was rewritten and must be recloned
questions.explanation: The old commits are not in the rewritten history, so Git reports something like ahead 2, behind 3. A plain pull would merge both copies and duplicate the commits, which is why published history should not be rewritten.

questions.text:
The shared repository on the server was created with plain git init and has main checked out. What happens when a developer runs the push below?

git push origin main
options: The push succeeds and the server's working tree is updated to the new commit
The push is refused with [remote rejected] main -> main (branch is currently checked out)
The push succeeds, but the server's checked-out files silently go stale
The push is refused as non-fast-forward until someone runs git pull on the server
questions.explanation: By default receive.denyCurrentBranch refuses updates to the branch checked out in a non-bare repository, because its index and working tree would no longer match. Shared remotes should be bare (git init --bare).

questions.text:
The server repo was created with sudo git init --bare /opt/git/myrepo.git, and root has no init.defaultBranch set. A developer whose config sets init.defaultBranch=main runs the commands below (Git 2.43 on both sides). What happens at the push?

git clone git@yourserver:/opt/git/myrepo.git && cd myrepo
echo hello > README.md && git add README.md && git commit -m "Initial commit"
git push origin main
options: The push creates main on the server and the server's HEAD switches to it
The push creates main, and later clones check it out without any warning
The push is rejected because an empty bare repository refuses its first push
It fails with error: src refspec main does not match any, because the clone's branch is master
questions.explanation: Cloning an empty repository adopts the server's unborn HEAD (refs/heads/master here), so the commit lands on local master. Creating the server repo with git init --bare --initial-branch=main avoids the mismatch.

questions.text: Which remote URL makes Git connect as git@yourserver and open the same repository as ssh://git@yourserver/opt/git/myrepo.git?
options: git@yourserver:/opt/git/myrepo.git
git@yourserver:opt/git/myrepo.git
git@yourserver/opt/git/myrepo.git
ssh://yourserver:git/opt/git/myrepo.git
questions.explanation: In scp-like syntax the path after the colon is passed as-is, so :opt/... is relative to the git user's home directory. Without any colon, Git treats the string as a local path and never uses SSH.

questions.text:
The git user's login shell is /usr/bin/git-shell. A developer with an authorised key runs the command below. What is the result?

ssh git@yourserver 'ls -la'
options: A listing of the git user's home directory, after which the connection closes
Permission denied (publickey), because git-shell rejects every SSH login
fatal: unrecognized command 'ls -la', while git clone and git push still work
An interactive restricted shell that allows only cd and ls
questions.explanation: git-shell accepts only Git's server-side commands such as git-upload-pack and git-receive-pack, so ordinary commands are refused while fetching and pushing keep working.

questions.text:
The server's pre-receive hook exits with status 1. A developer pushes two branches at once. What ends up on the server?

git push origin main feat
options: feat is created and only main is rejected, because it is listed first
Both refs are updated, and the hook's exit status is reported as a warning
main is updated and feat is rejected, because it is a new branch
Neither ref is updated; both are shown as (pre-receive hook declined)
questions.explanation: pre-receive runs once for the whole push, reading every <old> <new> <ref> line on stdin; a non-zero exit rejects all of them. Use the update hook for per-ref decisions.

questions.text: The server has an update hook that exits 1 when its first argument is refs/heads/main and 0 otherwise. What happens when a developer runs git push origin main feat, where feat is a new branch?
options: Both refs are rejected, because pushes are all-or-nothing by default
Both refs are updated, because update hooks can only print warnings
feat is created and main is rejected with (hook declined)
main is rejected and feat is skipped without being sent
questions.explanation: update runs once per ref, with the ref name and old and new IDs as arguments, so it can reject individual refs. A push is only all-or-nothing when you use git push --atomic.

questions.text: A post-receive hook runs a deploy script that fails, and the hook exits with status 1. What does the developer who pushed see?
