options: ! [remote rejected] main -> main (post-receive hook declined), and the ref stays put
The hook's output prefixed with remote:, and a successful main -> main update
A rejected push that Git retries automatically once the hook succeeds
The ref update is rolled back on the server and git push exits non-zero
questions.explanation: post-receive runs after all refs have been updated, so it cannot reject anything; its output is relayed with a remote: prefix and git push still exits 0. Validation belongs in pre-receive or update.

questions.text: After an admin runs find /opt/git -type f -exec chmod 644 {} \; on the server, pushes to main stop triggering the post-receive deploy. Why?
options: Hooks must be owned by root, and the command changed their owner
The hook now fails with Permission denied, so every push is rejected
Hooks without the execute bit are skipped, so the push succeeds but nothing runs
Hooks only run from .git/hooks, which a bare repository does not have
questions.explanation: Git runs a hook only if the file is executable; otherwise it ignores the hook and the push proceeds normally. Restore the bit with chmod +x /opt/git/myrepo.git/hooks/post-receive.

questions.text: You serve repositories with git daemon --base-path=/opt/git /opt/git and add a git-daemon-export-ok file to myrepo.git, so clones over git:// work. What happens when someone pushes to that git:// URL?
options: The push succeeds without authentication, because git:// has no access control
The push succeeds only if the user's SSH key is in authorized_keys
It fails with access denied or repository not exported, because only fetching is enabled
It fails until the repository also contains a git-daemon-push-ok file
questions.explanation: git daemon enables only the upload-pack (fetch) service by default; receive-pack must be enabled explicitly, which is rarely wise on an unauthenticated protocol. Push over SSH or authenticated HTTPS instead.

questions.text: Nginx forwards /git/ to git-http-backend with GIT_HTTP_EXPORT_ALL set and no authentication, and clones work. What happens when a developer pushes to that HTTP URL?
options: The server answers 403 Forbidden, because pushes need an authenticated user by default
The push succeeds, because GIT_HTTP_EXPORT_ALL enables both fetch and push
Git retries the push over SSH using the same host name
The push succeeds, but server-side hooks are skipped for HTTP pushes
questions.explanation: git-http-backend enables receive-pack only when the web server sets REMOTE_USER (an authenticated request) or http.receivepack is turned on, so anonymous pushes are refused. Put authentication in front of the location to allow pushes.

questions.text: The mirror remote has branches main and stale. Locally you have branches main and b1 and a tag v1. What does git push --mirror mirror do?
options: Pushes main, b1 and v1, and leaves stale untouched
Pushes main, b1 and v1, and deletes stale on the remote
Pushes only branches, because tags need a separate git push --tags
Refuses to run, because stale would be lost without --force
questions.explanation: --mirror makes the remote's refs match the local ones exactly: new and changed refs are pushed (force-updated if needed) and refs that no longer exist locally are deleted, shown as - [deleted] stale.

questions.text: Your team uses Git Flow. Production runs v2.3.0 from main, and develop already contains unreleased features. A critical bug is reported in production. What is the Git Flow way to fix it?
options: Commit the fix on develop and cut release/2.3.1 from it
Commit the fix directly on main, tag it, and leave develop alone
Branch feature/fix-bug from develop and ship it with the next release
Branch hotfix/2.3.1 from main, then merge it into main (tagged) and develop
questions.explanation: Hotfix branches start from the production line so unreleased work on develop is not shipped by accident; merging back into develop (or an active release branch) keeps the bug from returning in the next release.

questions.text: In Git Flow, release/1.4 has been cut from develop and QA is testing it. A developer finishes a new feature that was not planned for 1.4. Where should it be merged?
options: Into develop, so it ships with the next release
Into release/1.4, as long as its tests pass
Directly into main, so it bypasses the frozen release
Into a hotfix/* branch that is merged into the release
questions.explanation: Once a release branch is cut, only stabilisation work (bug fixes, docs, version bumps) goes on it. New features keep landing on develop and wait for the next release branch.

questions.text: Your team practises trunk-based development. A feature will take two weeks, but work must merge to main at least daily and main must stay releasable. What is the standard approach?
options: Keep a long-lived feature/* branch and merge it once at the end
Merge small increments daily behind a feature flag that is off by default
Push daily to a shared develop branch and merge that into main monthly
Merge to main daily but skip CI on commits that are unfinished
questions.explanation: Trunk-based development keeps branches short and hides incomplete behaviour behind flags (or branch by abstraction), so every commit on trunk builds, passes tests and is safe to deploy.

questions.text: Which description matches GitHub flow rather than Git Flow?
options: Permanent main and develop branches, plus release/* and hotfix/* branches
One long-lived branch per environment, promoted by merging upward
Everyone commits straight to main, with no branches and no reviews
A single always-deployable main, with short-lived branches merged via pull request
questions.explanation: GitHub flow uses only main plus short-lived topic branches that are reviewed in a pull request, merged and deployed. It has no develop, release/* or hotfix/* branches.

questions.text:
You maintain release/1.x alongside main. A bug fix was committed on main as 412cc26, and you run the commands below. What does the new commit's message look like?

git switch release/1.x
git cherry-pick -x 412cc26
options: The original message, and the new commit keeps the hash 412cc26
The original message followed by (cherry picked from commit 412cc26...)
Merge commit '412cc26' into release/1.x
The original message followed by a Signed-off-by: line naming you
questions.explanation: -x appends a line recording the source commit, which makes a fix traceable across release branches. The new commit has a different parent, so its hash differs from 412cc26.

questions.text: A team keeps qa, staging and production branches and promotes code by merging, cherry-picking hotfixes between them. What is the main criticism of this setup?
options: Git cannot merge between more than two long-lived branches
It forces every change to be hidden behind a feature flag
Environments end up running different commits, breaking "build once, promote the same artifact"
Production must be marked with lightweight tags, which cannot be signed
questions.explanation: Environment branches drift apart through merges and cherry-picks, so the commit tested in staging is not the one that reaches production. Promote a single build and keep environment differences in configuration.

questions.text: In your clone of a fork, origin is your fork and upstream is the canonical project. Your feat branch is behind upstream's main. Which commands bring it up to date?
options: git pull origin main, then git push upstream feat
git fetch upstream, then git rebase upstream/main
git fetch origin, then git rebase origin/main
git remote set-url origin <upstream-url>, then git pull
questions.explanation: New upstream commits only reach your clone by fetching from upstream; your fork's origin/main stays stale until you sync it. Rebasing onto upstream/main replays your work on the latest canonical history.

questions.text: A teammate pushed to develop a minute ago. You run git fetch origin develop before rebasing your feature branch. Where is the new tip of develop recorded?
options: Only in FETCH_HEAD; origin/develop is updated only by a plain git fetch
In your local develop branch, which fetch fast-forwards automatically
In both FETCH_HEAD and origin/develop, so git rebase origin/develop sees it
Nowhere yet, because fetch with a branch name only checks for updates
questions.explanation: Fetching a named branch writes FETCH_HEAD and also updates the matching remote-tracking ref, shown as develop -> origin/develop. Fetch never moves your local branches.

questions.text: A function in a shared library is renamed, and five services call it. Which property of a monorepo helps most with this change?
options: Each service can keep the old name until it opts into a new library version
The rename and every call-site update can land in one atomic commit
Clones are smaller, because each service is downloaded separately
Each service can be released on a fully independent schedule
questions.explanation: With everything in one repository, a cross-cutting refactor is one reviewed, revertible commit. In a multirepo the library is published first and each consumer is updated separately; the other options describe multirepo strengths.

questions.text:
You add a library as a submodule at libs/lib and commit. What does the command below print for that path?

git ls-tree HEAD libs/
options: 160000 commit <hash> libs/lib, a pointer to one commit of the library
040000 tree <hash> libs/lib, listing all of the library's files
100644 blob <hash> libs/lib, a file containing the library's URL
120000 blob <hash> libs/lib, a symlink to .git/modules/lib
questions.explanation: A submodule is stored as a gitlink: a tree entry with mode 160000 naming one commit in the other repository. The URL lives separately in .gitmodules.

questions.text: A teammate clones that superproject with a plain git clone. What do they find at libs/lib, and what fixes it?
options: The library's latest default-branch files, so nothing needs fixing
A broken symlink, which git submodule sync repairs
An empty directory; git submodule update --init checks out the recorded commit
A file holding the URL; git submodule add must be run again
questions.explanation: A plain clone does not fetch submodules, and git submodule status shows them with a leading -. Run git submodule update --init (or clone with --recurse-submodules) to clone them at the commit the superproject records.

questions.text: After git submodule update --init, a developer runs git status inside libs/lib. What is the first line of output?
options: On branch main
On branch libs/lib
fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git
HEAD detached at 53ed6ef
questions.explanation: git submodule update checks out the exact commit recorded in the superproject's gitlink, not a branch, so the submodule is in detached HEAD. Switch to a branch before committing inside it.

questions.text: A library was added with git subtree add --prefix=libs/lib <url> main --squash. What does a teammate get from a plain git clone of the app repository?
options: An empty libs/lib until they run git subtree pull
A gitlink at libs/lib that needs git submodule update --init
The library's files in libs/lib as ordinary tracked files
A .gitsubtree file that the clone uses to fetch the library
questions.explanation: A subtree merges the library's content into the repository's own history (here as one squashed commit), so clones get ordinary files with no extra steps. Only maintainers pulling upstream updates need git subtree.

questions.text:
A monorepo has README.md, apps/, libs/ and services/ at the top level. You run the command below. Which files remain in the working tree?

git sparse-checkout set services/payments
options: Only the files under services/payments/
README.md and other top-level files, plus everything under services/payments/
Everything under services/, but nothing from the top level
Every file, but only those under services/payments/ are writable
questions.explanation: set uses cone mode by default, which always keeps files directly in the root (and in each parent directory) plus the chosen directories recursively. The other files stay tracked in the index but are not written to disk.

questions.text:
You want a quick one-commit copy of a large repository on your own disk and run the command below. What do you get?

git clone --depth 1 mono mono-shallow
options: A full clone, with the warning --depth is ignored in local clones; use file:// instead.
A shallow clone with one commit, created with hard links
An error, because --depth only works with an ssh:// or https:// URL
A clone with one commit but no working tree
questions.explanation: Cloning from a plain local path copies or hard-links the object store directly, which ignores --depth. Use file:///path/to/mono so the clone goes through the transport and the shallow clone works.

questions.text: What is the key difference between git clone --filter=blob:none <url> and git clone --depth 1 <url>?
options: The filtered clone has only the newest commit; the shallow clone has every commit but no blobs
Both have full history; the filter only skips files above a size limit
The filtered clone never has file contents, so git checkout fails
The filtered clone has all commits and trees and fetches blobs on demand; the shallow clone truncates history
questions.explanation: A blob-less partial clone keeps complete history, so git log works, and downloads file contents when checkout or diff needs them. A depth-1 clone has a single grafted commit until you run git fetch --unshallow.

questions.text: echo 'hello world' | git hash-object --stdin prints 3b18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad. Which command prints the same hash?
options: printf 'hello world\n' | sha1sum
printf 'blob 11\0hello world' | sha1sum
printf 'blob 12\0hello world\n' | sha1sum
printf 'hello.txt\0hello world\n' | sha1sum
questions.explanation: An object ID is the SHA-1 of a header (type, space, byte length, NUL byte) followed by the content. echo adds a newline, making the content 12 bytes, and file names are never part of a blob.

questions.text:
In an empty repository you run the commands below. What does the last command print?

echo 'hello world' > hello.txt
git hash-object hello.txt
git cat-file -t 3b18e512
options: blob
file
3b18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad
fatal: Not a valid object name 3b18e512
questions.explanation: Without -w, git hash-object only computes the ID and writes nothing to .git/objects. After git hash-object -w hello.txt (or git add), git cat-file -t prints blob.

questions.text: You run git add notes.txt in a new repository but do not commit. Which statement is true?
options: Nothing is written to .git/objects until git commit runs
A blob for the content already exists in .git/objects, and the index points to it
The index itself stores a full copy of the file's contents
A blob, a tree and a commit are written, but no branch points to them yet
questions.explanation: Staging writes (or reuses) the blob immediately and records the path, mode and blob ID in the index. git commit later writes the tree and commit objects and moves the branch.

questions.text:
greeting.txt is already committed. You run the commands below. How many new objects does git add write?

cp greeting.txt copy.txt
git add copy.txt
options: None; the index entry for copy.txt points at the existing blob
One blob for the contents of copy.txt
One blob for copy.txt and one tree for the directory
One blob, one tree and one commit
questions.explanation: Identical bytes produce an identical blob ID, so both index entries share one blob. The new name only appears in a tree object when you commit.

questions.text: hello.txt sits in the repository root. You run git mv hello.txt greeting.txt and commit. How many new objects does the commit add?
options: One: a rename record pointing at the old blob
Three: a new blob, a new root tree and the commit
Two: a new root tree and the commit, reusing the existing blob
Four: a new blob, two new trees and the commit
questions.explanation: Names live in trees, so a rename changes only the root tree while the content blob is reused. Git stores no rename objects; rename detection is computed later by git diff or git log.

questions.text: You change one line in src/main.py, the only change, and commit. Which new objects are created?
options: A delta object for main.py and a commit
A new blob and a commit, with the existing trees updated in place
A new blob, a new src tree and a commit
A new blob, a new src tree, a new root tree and a commit
questions.explanation: Objects are immutable and a tree's ID depends on its entries, so a new blob forces new trees all the way up to the root. Unchanged sibling blobs and trees are reused.

questions.text: You run chmod +x deploy.sh without editing its contents and commit. What changes in the object database?
options: A new blob, because the file mode is part of the blob header
A new tree listing the same blob with mode 100755, plus a new commit
Nothing, because Git ignores permission changes unless you use --chmod
Only the index entry changes, so there is nothing to commit
questions.explanation: A blob holds only bytes, while the tree entry records the mode, so the same blob ID reappears under mode 100755. Git only ignores the change if core.fileMode is false.

questions.text:
You run the commands below in a clean repository. What does git status --short print?

mkdir empty
git add empty
git status --short
options: A empty/
?? empty/
fatal: pathspec 'empty' did not match any files
Nothing
questions.explanation: The index and trees record files (and gitlinks), and a directory exists in a tree only when it contains something. An empty directory is invisible to Git, which is why projects add a placeholder such as .gitkeep.

questions.text: A loose blob has the ID 3b18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad. Where is it stored?
options: .git/objects/3b/18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad
.git/objects/3b18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad
.git/objects/blob/3b18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad
.git/refs/objects/3b/18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad
questions.explanation: Loose objects are fanned out into subdirectories named after the first two hex characters of the ID, with the remaining 38 characters as the file name. The object type is stored inside the object, not in the path.

questions.text: You run cat on that loose object file. Why is the output unreadable?
options: It is encrypted with a key stored in .git/config
It holds a delta against another version of the file
It is the zlib-compressed bytes of blob 12\0hello world\n, header included
It is stored in the same binary format as .git/index
questions.explanation: Each loose object is its header plus content, compressed with zlib. Read it with git cat-file -p (content) or -t and -s (type and size); deltas are only used inside packfiles.

questions.text:
You create two tags on the same commit as shown. What do the two cat-file commands print?

git tag light
git tag -a v1 -m "first release"
git cat-file -t light
git cat-file -t v1
options: tag, then tag
commit, then commit
tag, then commit
commit, then tag
questions.explanation: A lightweight tag is only a ref pointing at the commit, while an annotated tag's ref points at a tag object that stores the tagger, date, message and target commit.

questions.text: For the annotated tag v1 from the previous question, which statement about git rev-parse v1 and git rev-parse v1^{commit} is true?
options: They print different IDs: first the tag object's, then the tagged commit's
They print the same ID, because a tag is only an alias for a commit
The first fails, because annotated tags must be peeled with ^{}
The second prints the ID of the tag's own tree
questions.explanation: refs/tags/v1 stores the tag object's ID; ^{commit} (or ^{}) peels the tag to the commit it points at, the same ID shown on the object line of git cat-file -p v1.

questions.text: You commit, then run git commit --amend -m "two" without changing any files. Which statement is true?
options: The commit ID stays the same, because the snapshot is unchanged
The tree ID changes, because the message is stored in the tree
The existing commit object is rewritten in place with the new message
The tree ID is unchanged, but a new commit object with a new ID is created
questions.explanation: A commit's ID covers its tree, parents, author, committer (with timestamps) and message, so a new message means a new commit. The old commit is untouched and stays reachable from the reflog as HEAD@{1}.

questions.text:
You run git checkout --detach and then the commands below. What do they print?

cat .git/HEAD
git symbolic-ref HEAD
options: ref: refs/heads/main, then refs/heads/main
A raw commit ID, then fatal: ref HEAD is not a symbolic ref
ref: HEAD, then HEAD
A raw commit ID, then refs/heads/main
questions.explanation: Normally .git/HEAD is a symbolic ref (ref: refs/heads/main). When detached it holds a commit ID directly, so git symbolic-ref HEAD fails; git symbolic-ref -q HEAD fails silently, which is handy in scripts.

questions.text: In a fresh clone whose remote default branch is main, what does git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD print?
options: refs/remotes/origin/main
origin/main
ref: refs/heads/main
The commit ID at the tip of origin/main
questions.explanation: origin/HEAD is a symbolic ref recording the remote's default branch; its file contains ref: refs/remotes/origin/main and symbolic-ref prints the full target. git rev-parse --abbrev-ref origin/HEAD would print origin/main.

questions.text: A deploy script runs cat .git/refs/heads/main to get the current commit. After git gc it fails with No such file or directory, yet git log main still works. What is the robust fix?
options: Run git checkout main before the script so the file is recreated
Read .git/HEAD instead, because it always contains a commit ID
Use git rev-parse refs/heads/main, which also reads .git/packed-refs
Turn off ref packing by running git gc --no-prune instead
questions.explanation: git gc packs refs into .git/packed-refs and removes the loose ref files. Commands such as git rev-parse resolve both loose and packed refs, so scripts should not read ref files directly.

questions.text: A repository contains only loose objects, all reachable. You run git gc and then git count-objects -v. What do you expect?
options: count: 0, with every object counted under in-pack in a .pack file indexed by an .idx
An unchanged count, because gc only deletes unreachable objects
count: 0 and in-pack: 0, because gc deletes objects that were already pushed
packs: 0, because packfiles are only created by git push and git fetch
questions.explanation: gc repacks reachable objects into a packfile, which uses delta compression to save space, plus an .idx index for fast lookup. Objects are never deleted just because a remote also has them.

questions.text: You amended a commit a minute ago and then ran git gc. Is the pre-amend commit still in the repository?
options: Yes; the reflog still references it, so gc keeps it
No; gc deletes every commit not reachable from a branch or tag
No; --amend deleted the old commit immediately
Yes, but only as a loose file that git cat-file cannot read
questions.explanation: Reflog entries count as reachability roots, and gc prunes unreachable objects only after a grace period (two weeks by default), so recent rewrites can be recovered with git reflog.

questions.text:
You stage a file, edit it, and stage it again without committing. What does git fsck report?

echo v1 > d && git add d
echo v2 > d && git add d
git fsck
options: Nothing, because the second git add overwrote the first blob in place
dangling blob <hash>, for the blob holding v1
missing blob <hash>, because the index lost a reference
dangling commit <hash>, because each git add creates a commit
questions.explanation: The first git add wrote a blob that no index entry, tree or ref references any more, so fsck lists it as dangling. gc prunes such objects once they are older than the grace period.

questions.text: You committed a secret, ran git reset --hard HEAD~1, and have not pushed. Which command sequence removes the commit from the local object database right away?
options: git gc
git prune
git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now
git reset --hard HEAD~1 && git gc --aggressive
questions.explanation: The reflog still references the commit, so gc and prune keep it. Expiring the reflog makes it unreachable, and --prune=now deletes unreachable objects without waiting for the grace period.

questions.text:
You build a commit with plumbing commands as shown. Why does git log not list it?

tree=$(git write-tree)
git commit-tree "$tree" -p HEAD -m "manual"
git log --oneline
options: commit-tree only prints a preview and then discards the object
write-tree needs git add -A first, so the commit was empty
The commit becomes visible only after git gc packs it
The commit exists, but no ref points to it until git update-ref moves one
questions.explanation: write-tree writes a tree from the index and commit-tree writes a commit and prints its ID, but neither moves a branch. git update-ref refs/heads/main <id> is the step that makes it part of main.

questions.text: On main, git merge x stops with a conflict in a. What does git cat-file -p :2:a print?
options: The version of a from main (ours)
The common ancestor's version of a
The version of a from x (theirs)
The working-tree file with conflict markers
questions.explanation: During a conflict the index holds stage 1 (base), stage 2 (ours, the branch you are on) and stage 3 (theirs), all visible with git ls-files -s. The file with markers exists only in the working tree.
